## The pilot found lower waste costs {#d3s1-p01 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(interval_svg('trial'))
```

The lottery assigned **200 businesses to GreenWaste** and **200 to the control group** in one pilot district. At 12 months, annual waste management cost was **`r fmt(model$saving)` AED lower per business** in the treatment group.

::: {.ask}
What does the interval tell us about the separate **1,000 AED annual-saving rule**?
:::

::: {.notes}
**4 minutes. Main point:** The pilot RCT supplies an estimated effect on annual waste cost, not a programme-delivery cost.

- Retrieve the Day 1 pilot: 400 businesses in one district, assigned by lottery. The treatment-minus-control estimate is -1,014 AED in annual waste cost at 12 months. On a saving scale, the 95% interval is 862 to 1,167 AED.
- The point estimate exceeds the 1,000 AED rule, but the interval crosses it. This does not settle the minimum-saving decision. Keep the unit as AED per business per year, and the population as the pilot district.
- Ask what the trial did not measure for today's spending question. It did not provide a full incremental programme cost or evidence that the effect persists for five years.
:::

## Measured saving, assumed programme cost {#d3s1-p02 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<div class="evidence-pair">
<div><span class="evidence-label">RCT estimate at 12 months</span><strong>`r fmt(model$saving)` AED</strong><span>lower annual waste cost per pilot business</span></div>
<div><span class="evidence-label">Economic model assumption</span><strong>`r fmt(model$cost)` AED</strong><span>delivery cost per business, paid at year 0</span></div>
</div>

The **1,800 AED is not an RCT result**. We would need programme accounts to establish its amount and what it includes.

::: {.ask}
Can we decide whether the programme pays for itself by comparing 1,014 with 1,800 once?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** Impact evidence and cost evidence are distinct inputs.

- Point left to the trial estimate and right to the assumed delivery cost. The trial compares outcomes under GreenWaste with outcomes under no GreenWaste. The 1,800 AED is fictional and has no cost audit behind it.
- Ask why 1,014 divided by 1,800 would mislead: one is an annual rate at 12 months, the other a one-off year-0 cost. We need a time horizon, evidence on persistence and a common valuation date.
- Ask each table to name the source of both numbers: trial data for the saving; an assumption for delivery cost. Take one answer aloud before moving on. Running R cannot turn an assumed cost into a measured cost.
:::

## Economic evaluation compares alternatives {#d3s1-p03 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_rct_means_chart())
```

The RCT compares **GreenWaste versus no GreenWaste** in the pilot district. An appraisal then adds the **incremental programme cost**, for the same alternative, population and period.

The bars show the measured outcome; they do **not** include the cost of delivering GreenWaste.

::: {.ask}
If control businesses also pay for waste collection, should their ordinary collection costs become a new GreenWaste programme cost?
:::

::: {.notes}
**4 minutes. Main point:** The trial comparison gives an outcome difference; the appraisal needs an incremental delivery-cost ledger for that same comparison.

- Point to the two 12-month group means: GreenWaste businesses had lower average annual waste cost. Their difference is 1,014 AED per business. The RCT control group represents the pilot's no-GreenWaste alternative. Count additional resources caused by GreenWaste, not every expense either group already had.
- Ordinary waste-management costs are the measured outcome in this trial. A separate programme-cost ledger would show equipment, staff, administration, business time and maintenance as relevant to the chosen perspective, avoiding double counting.
- Ask what changes when the decision shifts from the pilot to a citywide rollout. Costs, uptake and effects may all change. The pilot comparison alone cannot answer that larger question.
:::

## Three ways to compare costs and results {#d3s1-p04 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<p class="d3-screen-instruction">At your table, say what decision each result could help with. Open the cards to see the method names.</p>

<div class="d3-method-cards">
<details><summary>AED per tonne of landfill avoided</summary><p><strong>CEA:</strong> cost per additional result, measured in its natural unit.</p></details>
<details><summary>AED per year in good health</summary><p><strong>CUA:</strong> cost per QALY gained. A QALY combines years lived and health quality.</p></details>
<details><summary>Net benefit in AED</summary><p><strong>CBA:</strong> put the included benefits and costs into money, then compare them.</p></details>
</div>

**CUA is a specialised form of CEA.** The question and available outcome data determine the method.

::: {.ask}
Which approach can use GreenWaste's measured waste-cost outcome in a monetary model?
:::

::: {.notes}
**6 minutes. Main point:** The methods differ in the unit used for the result. All compare added costs and added outcomes against an alternative.

- Give tables one minute to discuss what each result could help decide, then open each card and introduce the name. CEA keeps the result in its natural unit; CUA uses a health measure called a QALY; CBA puts included benefits and costs in money.
- GreenWaste's RCT outcome is already measured in AED, so it can be a candidate monetary benefit in a partial cost-benefit model after checking what the spending represents. A landfill outcome in tonnes would support a separate CEA if its causal effect and incremental costs were estimated. No QALY is in this case.
- For definitions, see the [CDC's CEA guide](https://www.cdc.gov/polaris/php/economics/cost-effectiveness.html), [NICE's cost-utility guidance](https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2/), and the [HM Treasury Green Book](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-green-book--2/the-green-book-2026). These are methodological references; the case's 5% rate is an assumption, not official guidance.
:::

## Cost per tonne of landfill avoided {#d3s1-p05 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<div class="method-equation"><div class="fraction"><span>extra cost of GreenWaste</span><span>extra tonnes of landfill avoided</span></div><strong>= AED per tonne avoided</strong></div>

This keeps the outcome in **tonnes**. We would need a credible estimate of the programme's effect on landfill and a complete incremental cost for the same businesses and period.

::: {.ask}
Would the RCT's 1,014 AED waste-cost saving fill the denominator of this CEA?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** CEA answers a cost-per-natural-outcome question, so the denominator must match the outcome named.

- The denominator here is tonnes of landfill avoided relative to the no-GreenWaste alternative. The 1,014 AED RCT result concerns waste-management cost and cannot be relabelled as tonnes.
- For some perspectives, avoided waste spending could lower the net incremental cost in the numerator. The evaluator must check whether that spending is a real resource saving or a transfer, and avoid including it again as a separate monetary benefit in the same calculation.
- Give tables one minute to name the two missing records: landfill outcomes for both groups and complete programme costs. Do not calculate an AED-per-tonne figure from invented effects.
:::

## Cost per QALY gained in a health study {#d3s1-p06 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_qaly_chart())
```

A **QALY** combines years lived and health-related quality of life. CUA divides extra cost by extra QALYs gained. This diagram is a separate health example: GreenWaste has **no measured QALY outcome**.

::: {.ask}
Why would tonnes of landfill avoided and QALYs answer different policy questions?
:::

::: {.notes}
**4 minutes. Main point:** CUA is useful when the decision turns on health-related quality and length of life measured on a common utility scale.

- Read the shaded area: four years at a quality-of-life weight of 0.7 give 2.8 QALYs in this simplified health example. It is not a GreenWaste finding. Explain that CUA is a specialised CEA, usually expressed as incremental cost per QALY gained against an alternative.
- The case has neither a measured health-utility outcome nor a credible causal pathway quantified into QALYs. Do not convert waste cost or landfill tonnes into QALYs by assertion.
- Ask tables why landfill tonnes and years in good health answer different questions. Take one example aloud. [NICE's economic evaluation manual](https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2/) gives a primary example of cost-utility analysis.
:::

## Are the money benefits larger than the costs? {#d3s1-p07 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<div class="equation-row"><span>savings valued today</span><strong>minus</strong><span>costs valued today</span><strong>= net benefit (AED)</strong></div>

Or divide savings by costs to get a **benefit-cost ratio**. A ratio above **1** means the savings included in this model exceed its included costs.

GreenWaste's waste-cost saving is in AED. A lower bill is a gain for society only if it reflects fewer real resources used, not just a payment moved from one group to another.

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** A benefit-cost ratio is meaningful only for a stated boundary of monetised benefits and costs.

- Explain both measures without treating them as interchangeable: net present benefit is an amount of AED; the ratio has no units. Both compare present values over the same period.
- A business bill reduction can reflect saved resources, lower charges, or both. A transfer between actors is not automatically a net gain for society. The worked model is deliberately partial and mixes an authority cost with a business financial outcome.
- This is not a complete social CBA or an authority budget return. Use [HM Treasury's Green Book guidance on economic transfers and perspectives](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-green-book--2/the-green-book-2026) as a methodological reference.
:::

## Whose costs and savings count? {#d3s1-p08 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<div class="perspective-lines"><p><strong>Authority:</strong> equipment, delivery staff, administration and any public savings.</p><p><strong>Businesses:</strong> waste spending, staff time and maintenance.</p><p><strong>Society:</strong> all real resources used or saved, plus environmental effects. A payment moved between groups is not a new social gain.</p></div>

The current illustration includes **one assumed authority cost** and **one business financial saving**. It leaves other entries unmeasured.

::: {.ask}
Could the director call this ratio a return on the authority's budget?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** The decision maker must choose a perspective before declaring which costs and benefits count.

- Read the authority and business lines aloud. The model combines an authority delivery cost with a business waste-cost saving. The latter does not automatically return money to the authority's budget.
- For a social analysis, determine whether reduced bills reflect saved collection resources or transfers to someone else. Ask for staff time, maintenance, implementation and environmental effects, with timing and ownership of each item.
- Ask each table to name one missing cost or benefit and the record that would establish it. Hear one authority item and one business item. Avoid adding a guessed amount twice.
:::

## The model assumes five years of savings {#d3s1-p09 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_timeline())
```

**Year 0:** assumed 1,800 AED delivery cost. **Years 1-5:** model the RCT's annual saving of about 1,014 AED each year.

Only the **12-month annual-cost effect** comes from the RCT. The same saving in later years is an assumption.

::: {.ask}
Which part of this timeline would follow-up data test?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** The five-year stream is a forecast built from one RCT estimate.

- The RCT measures annual waste cost at 12 months, not a five-year cash-flow series. For this teaching illustration, the model treats that annual difference as the saving in year 1 and repeats it in years 2 to 5.
- The 1,800 AED cost occurs in year 0 as an assumption. No audited cost schedule or follow-up evidence for persistence is supplied.
- Ask tables which part was observed at 12 months and which years are projected. Follow-up data would test fading benefits; programme accounts would reveal maintenance costs.
:::

## A future saving has a lower value today {#d3s1-p10 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_discount())
```

At the **assumed 5% rate**, the year-1 saving has a year-0 value of about **`r fmt(model$saving/1.05)` AED**. Later modelled savings receive larger discounts.

::: {.ask}
Does discounting tell us whether the forecast savings will actually happen?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** Discounting expresses future amounts in year-0 terms; it does not supply evidence that they will occur.

- Follow the plotted points from years 1 to 5. Each starts with the same assumed 1,014 AED annual saving, but its value at year 0 falls with time. Work the first point: 1,014.355 divided by 1.05 equals about 966 AED. The teaching calculation uses the unrounded RCT estimate; slides display whole AED.
- The 5% rate is a case assumption, not a rate that we claim an authority must use. The first modelled saving is year 1, aligned with the 12-month annual-cost outcome; years 2 to 5 remain forecasts.
- Ask tables to predict the year-1 value before showing the first plotted label. Work 1,014 divided by 1.05 on screen or aloud. Keep discounting separate from the assumption that benefits persist.
:::

## Five modelled savings have a present value of 4,392 AED {#d3s1-p11 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<div class="cash-table">
```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_cash_table())
```
</div>

Add the **year-1 to year-5 present values**, using the unrounded RCT estimate. The result is **`r fmt(d7_benefits)` AED per pilot business** under the model.

::: {.notes}
**6 minutes. Main point:** The total is a discounted forecast, not five observed RCT outcomes.

- Point to year 0: delivery cost 1,800 AED. Each of years 1 to 5 uses the same annual saving assumption but a different discount factor. Read year 1 and year 5; participants can scan the middle rows.
- Rounded displayed rows may differ by one AED from the rounded exact total. The helper calculates with the unrounded RCT estimate of 1,014.355 AED.
- Ask one table why multiplying 1,014 by five is not the value today, and another why five saving years cannot be inferred from a 12-month trial.
:::

## The partial model gives a ratio of 2.44 {#d3s1-p12 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_value_chart())
```

**Benefit-cost ratio:** `r fmt(d7_benefits)` / `r fmt(model$cost)` = **`r fmt(ratio(),2)`**. **Net present benefit:** `r fmt(d7_benefits)` - `r fmt(model$cost)` = **`r fmt(d7_npv)` AED**.

::: {.ask}
What does a ratio above 1 say here? What does it leave unproved?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** Under the stated limited model, discounted business savings exceed the assumed delivery cost.

- Read the chart: 4,392 AED in modelled benefits, 1,800 AED in assumed costs, and 2,592 AED net present benefit per pilot business. Their quotient is 2.44, with no units.
- This is a partial monetary comparison, not a complete social CBA or a return to the authority's budget. The RCT uncertainty, benefit persistence, full costs and pilot-to-city transfer remain unresolved.
- The 1,000 AED annual-saving rule is a separate outcome threshold. A ratio above one does not show that rule is met with confidence.
:::

## R reproduces the arithmetic, not the assumptions {#d3s1-p13 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{webr}
#| context: setup
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
#| include: false
gw <- read.csv('evaluation_data_GreenWaste_simple.csv')
pilot <- subset(gw, setting == 'pilot')
```

```{webr}
#| echo: true
# RCT difference in annual cost at 12 months: treatment minus control.
saving <- -(mean(pilot$cost_after[pilot$took_part == 1]) -
            mean(pilot$cost_after[pilot$took_part == 0]))
# Assumed delivery cost, five saving years and 5% discount rate.
benefits <- saving * sum(1 / 1.05^(1:5))
c(ratio = round(benefits / 1800, 2),
  net_AED = round(benefits - 1800))
```

**Measured in the trial:** 1,014 AED lower annual cost after 12 months. **Assumed for this model:** 1,800 AED delivery cost, five years of savings, and a 5% discount rate. R calculates a **2.44 ratio**; it cannot verify the assumptions.

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** The code uses the RCT effect but cannot validate assumed costs or persistence.

- Ask what comes from the file: the pilot's treatment and control mean annual costs at 12 months. The difference is the RCT estimate. The 1,800 AED delivery cost, five saving years and 5% rate are specified by us.
- Run the code once; participants need not code. Point to the measured-versus-assumed sentence below it. The output should show a ratio of 2.44 and net present benefit of 2,592 AED. If browser R is slow, state those results aloud.
- The model is per pilot business. Do not multiply by all city participants or label the output an observed financial return.
:::

## Break-even and the 1,000 AED rule are different {#d3s1-p14 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_break_even_chart())
```

Under **this model's** 1,800 AED cost, five years and 5% rate, an annual saving of about **`r fmt(model$cost/pv_factor())` AED** would give a ratio of 1. The separate **policy rule is 1,000 AED per year**.

::: {.ask}
Does the RCT interval settle either threshold? Which part of the model could move the break-even point?
:::

::: {.notes}
**6 minutes. Main point:** A model break-even saving and the policy's annual-saving minimum answer separate questions.

- The model break-even calculation is 1,800 divided by the five-year present-value factor, about 416 AED per year. It assumes all listed inputs and costs are correct. The pilot RCT interval of 862 to 1,167 AED is above this model threshold, but that is only partial uncertainty.
- The interval crosses the policy's 1,000 AED annual-saving rule. It therefore does not establish that the rule is exceeded with 95% confidence. Raising costs or shortening persistence moves the economic break-even saving upward.
- Do not turn the RCT confidence interval into a confidence interval for the ratio; cost, persistence and transfer beyond the pilot are also uncertain. Ask tables which threshold the interval crosses.
:::

## Which assumption changes the result? {#d3s1-p15 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

```{r, results='asis'}
html_out(d7_interactive_model())
```

<p class="d3-screen-instruction">Predict first. Then move one slider at a time. Finally combine fading savings with extra costs.</p>

::: {.ask}
Can you move the ratio below 1? Which input needs real evidence before a decision?
:::

::: {.notes}
**6 minutes. Main point:** The ratio changes when assumed cost or future savings change. The sliders test assumptions; they do not estimate what will happen.

- Ask tables to predict the direction of each slider before moving it. At the default, five years, no fading and no extra cost give 2.44. Three years give about 1.53; 30% annual fading gives about 1.40. Combining 30% fading and 800 AED extra cost gives about 0.97.
- Point to both bars: the blue bar is modelled savings, the red bar is assumed cost. The 5% discount rate stays fixed on this slide. Reset after the combined example.
- Ask for records: programme accounts and staff time for costs; follow-up waste-cost data for persistence. Each table names one record and how a different value would change its advice.
:::

## A pilot result does not price a citywide rollout {#d3s1-p16 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

The RCT covered **400 eligible businesses in one district**. A citywide decision may involve different businesses, delivery capacity, prices and take-up.

<div class="reach-lines"><p><strong>We have:</strong> a pilot effect on annual waste cost at 12 months.</p><p><strong>We need:</strong> credible rollout costs, follow-up on savings and evidence that the effect applies beyond the pilot.</p></div>

::: {.ask}
What would change if the same programme costs more per business at city scale?
:::

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** The worked ratio is per pilot business under assumptions, not a citywide forecast.

- Ask participants to name one way scale could change the numerator and one way it could change the denominator. New districts and businesses may respond differently; delivery capacity and input prices can also change.
- The RCT has a strong assignment comparison within its pilot, but external validity remains a separate question. The city DiD, RDD and matching exercises ask other questions and do not supply automatic independent confirmation of this pilot model.
- Ask each table for one specific record and how a different result would change its rollout advice.
:::

## Check an overconfident recommendation {#d3s1-p17 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

<blockquote class="claim">“The RCT proves GreenWaste saves 1,014 AED every year for five years. The programme costs 1,800 AED, so its benefit-cost ratio of 2.44 proves that citywide expansion is good value for money.”</blockquote>

::: {.ask}
Underline what the RCT supports. Cross out what the model assumes or what the pilot cannot establish.
:::

At your table, replace the claim with one sentence that separates **what the RCT found** from **what the model assumes**.

::: {.notes}
**5 minutes. Main point:** Correct arithmetic can sit inside an unsupported policy claim.

- Give two minutes for individual marking and two minutes for paired correction. The RCT supports an estimated 12-month difference for the pilot, with uncertainty. It does not show five years of constant savings or a measured 1,800 AED delivery cost.
- The ratio is conditional on a partial model. It does not establish a complete social return or a citywide effect. Ask one pair to replace “proves” with a precise statement about what the model suggests and what must be checked.
- This written claim is an authored critical-reading exercise, not a real AI output. The same verification habit applies to an AI summary or a human briefing.
:::

## What would you recommend? {#d3s1-p18 .reader-slide .s1-review .d3s1-review}

Give two sentences to your table:

1. What the pilot-based model suggests **under its stated assumptions**.
2. Your provisional action and the **specific evidence** that could change it.

A sound answer separates the **RCT effect**, the **assumed cost and persistence**, and the **decision at city scale**.

::: {.notes}
**4 minutes. Main point:** Participants should leave able to use an economic model without overstating the trial or the forecast.

- Give two minutes for table discussion, one minute for a partner to check units and scope, and one minute to hear a contrasting decision. An answer may request audited delivery costs, follow-up data, or evidence on transfer to other districts.
- Accept a conditional pilot extension, a delayed city decision, or another defensible action if the evidence request could realistically change it. Do not demand a single approve/reject answer.
- Recap the three methods: CEA uses a natural outcome, CUA uses health utility, and CBA monetises both sides. The partial GreenWaste ratio is a CBA-style illustration. A later mock report uses a separate city DiD model with a ratio of 1.86 and different timing assumptions; that is a document to critique, not another calculation of this pilot model. These notes total 90 minutes.
:::
